domain_name: Quality of the Internal Audit Function
source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 3 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section C is about how the chief audit executive proves and improves the function's own quality. It covers the quality assurance and improvement program with its internal and external assessments, honest disclosure when a requirement of the Standards is not met, and the performance measures the board and senior management use to judge the function.
analogy: Think of a hospital's surgical department. A senior surgeon checks each junior's work as it happens; once a year the department reviews its own records against clinical standards; every few years an outside accreditation team inspects it. When a rule could not be followed, say a staff shortage stopped a second check, the department records why, what it did instead and what that changed, and tells the hospital board. Outcome scorecards, not case counts alone, show whether it is improving.

parts.name: Quality of the Internal Audit Function

topics.overview: The quality assurance and improvement program is the chief audit executive's standing system for checking conformance with the Standards and progress on performance objectives, and for improving. This topic covers its parts, internal and external assessments, who may assess, and what the board must hear.
can_do: Explain what the quality program is for and name its internal and external parts
Describe what ongoing monitoring covers and what a periodic self-assessment adds
Compare internal with external assessments and recognize who qualifies as an independent assessor
Recognize what the CAE reports on quality, to whom and how often

subtopics.name: Purpose and Parts of the Quality Program
subtopics.definition: A quality assurance and improvement program is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) standing system of reviews that checks conformance with the Standards and progress on performance goals, and drives improvement.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Quality is what lets the board trust internal audit's conclusions. The program shows with evidence whether the function meets the Standards and its own goals.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 8.3 Quality): the CAE develops, implements and maintains a program covering every aspect of the function; Principle 12 defines quality as conformance plus performance.
Must: the program includes internal assessments (ongoing monitoring and periodic self-assessments, Standard 12.1) and external assessments (Standard 8.4).
KaiSip's reading: the purpose is to evaluate and promote conformance, performance and continuous improvement, not to award a pass mark.
Must: quality assessments evaluate conformance with Topical Requirements, so applicability records and exclusion reasons are kept for the assessors.
KaiSip's reading (Fundamentals): a one-person function still needs a program, and it will need help from outside the function.
subtopics.example: At a regional bank in Ghana, CAE Kofi inherits a function whose only quality step is a yearly survey. Kofi adds supervisory sign-off on every workpaper, a yearly self-assessment against each standard, kept Topical Requirement applicability records, and an external assessment booked for next year.

review: Inspect the program document for both internal and external parts
Trace last year's improvement actions to their completion
Sample assurance files for a record of each topical rule considered
evidence: Methodology section describing each assessment and its reporting
Latest self-review file with its conclusions on each standard
Improvement log with owners and completion dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive document a program that covers every part of the function, Topical Requirement conformance included.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive owns the program; the board discusses it with them

subtopics.isaca_rule: Quality means conformance plus performance. The program must cover the whole function through internal and external assessments. The CAE owns it and may delegate tasks, never the accountability.

exam_traps.trap: A strong external assessment every five years is the quality program.
exam_traps.why: The program must also include internal assessments, ongoing and periodic, reported to the board and senior management at least annually.

exam_traps.trap: Topical Requirements sit outside quality assessments because they are topic-specific.
exam_traps.why: Assurance work must follow any Topical Requirement in scope, and quality assessments check whether it did.

key_terms.definition: The CAE's program of internal and external assessments covering conformance, performance objectives and continuous improvement.
In the Standards' sense, meeting the Standards together with reaching the function's own performance goals.
The opening part of the Global Internal Audit Standards, explaining the framework and how to apply the Standards, small functions included.

subtopics.memory_aid: Quality is conformance plus performance, checked from inside and outside.

subtopics.name: The Two Layers of Internal Assessment
subtopics.definition: Internal assessments are the function's own quality checks: ongoing monitoring built into daily management, and periodic self-assessments that test conformance with every standard.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Waiting five years for outsiders is too slow. Internal assessments catch weak work while it can be fixed and prepare for the external assessment.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 12.1 Internal Quality Assessment): the chief audit executive (CAE) sets a method for ongoing monitoring, periodic self-assessments and reporting their results.
May (Standard 12.1 considerations): monitor through supervisory review of planning, workpapers and final communications, checklists, stakeholder surveys and metrics such as budget variance.

Sound practice (Standard 12.1 considerations): a periodic self-assessment covers every standard, the methodologies, support for objectives, quality of work and supervision, and stakeholder expectations.
Must: assessors are internal auditors or others in the organization who know internal audit practice well.
Should: involve staff in self-assessments to deepen their grasp of the Standards.
Must: turn self-assessment results into action plans with a proposed timeline, report both to the board and senior management, and document every internal assessment.

rows.label: When
cells: Continuously, inside daily management
At intervals, as a structured review

rows.label: Coverage
cells: Mainly the standards used in engagements
Every standard and the function as a whole

rows.label: Typical tools
cells: Supervisory review, checklists, surveys, metrics
Conformance rating per standard, interviews, surveys

rows.label: Who
cells: Supervisors and the CAE
Senior auditors, a quality team, or others with audit skills

subtopics.example: At a Mexican retail chain, supervisor Paola reviews each workpaper against a checklist before sign-off, and managers of audited areas get a short survey. Each year CAE Javier asks a senior auditor and an internal control specialist from finance to rate conformance with every standard, then sends the board an action plan with dates.

review: Sample engagements for dated supervisory sign-off and completed checklists
Inspect the last self-assessment for a rating against every standard
Trace self-assessment gaps to dated action plans
evidence: Workpaper review checklists showing reviewer and date
Signed rating sheet scoring the function standard by standard
Minutes showing the board and executives received the findings
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive schedule periodic self-assessments covering every standard and track each resulting action to completion.
audit_focus.decides: How the function checks itself is the CAE's call

subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal assessment has two layers: continuous monitoring inside daily work, and a periodic look at every standard. Must: document both, build action plans with timelines, and report results to the board and senior management.

exam_traps.trap: Ongoing monitoring and periodic self-assessment are the same review at different times.
exam_traps.why: Monitoring is built into daily supervision and centers on engagement work; periodic self-assessments are holistic and cover every standard.

exam_traps.trap: A self-assessment done with help from another department counts as an external assessment.
exam_traps.why: People elsewhere in the organization may help with internal assessments, but they are never independent enough for an external one.

key_terms.definition: The function's own check of its quality: ongoing monitoring plus periodic self-assessment, reported at least yearly.
A questionnaire asking those internal audit serves to rate its work; one input to ongoing monitoring.
A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.

subtopics.name: External Assessments and Qualified Assessors
subtopics.definition: An external quality assessment is an independent, qualified outside review of the whole internal audit function, required no less often than once in five years.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Self-review has limits. A qualified outside view tells the board whether the function truly conforms with the Standards.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 8.4 External Quality Assessment): an independent, qualified assessor or team reviews the function no less often than once in five years; independently validated self-assessment also qualifies.
Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) plans the assessment, discusses the plan with the board, and ensures at least one assessor holds an active Certified Internal Auditor (CIA) designation.
Essential condition (for the board or senior management, not a requirement on internal audit): the board approves the plan and receives the complete results directly from the assessor.
Should: also weigh Standards knowledge, senior audit leadership, industry and assessment experience, recognized training and a no-conflicts statement.
May: assess more often, for example after a change of leaders, a merger of functions or heavy turnover.

rows.label: Peer review
cells: Rotation among three or more peer organizations
Two organizations assessing each other

rows.label: Inside the group
cells: Nothing inside the organization or its group
Another department, a parent, an affiliate or an oversight body

rows.label: Public sector
cells: Not excluded by this test: bodies under separate audit heads
Same-tier bodies reporting to one CAE

rows.label: Other ties
cells: Weighed case by case
Possible impairment: financial statement audit, past help to internal audit, recent employment

subtopics.example: A Malaysian state-owned utility's audit committee asks for its first external assessment. CAE Nurul rejects a swap with a neighboring utility's team, since two-way reviews are not independent, and proposes an outside team with one active CIA. The committee approves the plan.

review: Compare the last external assessment's date with the five-year limit
Inspect assessor profiles for independence statements and active CIA status
Trace the proposal for the review to the minute that approved it
evidence: Board minutes approving the external assessment plan
Assessor team profiles with certifications and conflict attestations
Final report sent by the assessor directly to the board
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive plan the next external assessment early and confirm the assessors' independence and qualifications with the board.
audit_focus.decides: Board: signs off the proposal and gets the report unfiltered

subtopics.isaca_rule: At least once in five years, a qualified, independent assessor or team with at least one active CIA. The CAE plans and discusses; the board approves the plan and receives the full results directly.

exam_traps.trap: A review by the organization's compliance department meets the external assessment requirement.
exam_traps.why: Another department is separate from internal audit but not independent for this purpose.

exam_traps.trap: Every member of the assessment team must hold the CIA designation.
exam_traps.why: Must: at least one holds an active CIA. Other qualifications are considerations.

key_terms.definition: A full internal assessment that a qualified, independent outside assessor then validates; it can meet the external requirement.
Two organizations' internal audit functions assessing each other; not independent for an external assessment.
Board and senior management activities, not requirements on them, that Domain III lists as necessary for an effective internal audit function.
The Standards' third domain, on governing the internal audit function: Principles 6 to 8 and Standards 6.1 to 8.4.

subtopics.memory_aid: Every five years, outside, independent, one active CIA; the board approves and receives.

subtopics.name: Reporting Quality Results to the Board
subtopics.definition: Quality reporting is the chief audit executive (CAE) telling the board and senior management, on a set schedule, where the function stands on conformance, performance and improvement.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The board oversees internal audit and judges its effectiveness. Without regular, candid quality results it cannot tell whether the conclusions it receives deserve trust.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 8.3 Quality): report internal assessment results to the board and senior management at least annually, and external results when completed.
Must: each report says how far the function conforms and meets its performance objectives, plus, where they apply, legal compliance on internal auditing and plans to improve.
Should: say what each assessment covered, how often it runs and what it found, then the actions agreed with the board and how far they have got.
Must (Standard 12.1): disclose to the board and senior management any nonconformance affecting the function's overall scope or operation, with its impact.

Essential condition (for the board or senior management, not a requirement on internal audit): the board discusses the program, approves post-assessment action plans and timelines, and monitors progress.
subtopics.example: At an Australian pension fund, CAE Harper's annual quality report tells the board and senior management that two engagements lacked documented supervision and that 85 percent of the plan was completed. Harper presents an action plan with dates, the board agrees the timeline, and Harper reports progress at each quarterly meeting.

review: Compare quality report dates with the yearly reporting rule
Inspect each report for conformance, performance, compliance and improvement content
Trace agreed improvement actions to progress reported later
evidence: Minutes recording the board's discussion of the yearly report
Outside assessor's report together with the CAE's reply
Tracker of improvement actions with board-agreed timelines
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive give the board and senior management a yearly quality report with actions, dates and progress.
audit_focus.decides: The board agrees improvement actions and monitors progress

subtopics.isaca_rule: Report quality, good or bad: internal results at least annually, external results on completion, to the board and senior management. Include conformance, performance and improvement plans; a function-wide nonconformance is disclosed with its impact.

exam_traps.trap: Internal assessment results go to the board only when they reveal problems.
exam_traps.why: Must: results go to the board and senior management at least annually, whatever they show.

exam_traps.trap: Senior management receives the external results first and decides what the board sees.
exam_traps.why: Must: results are reported to the board and senior management, and the board receives the complete results directly from the assessor (an essential condition).

key_terms.definition: The CAE's dated actions to fix gaps that quality assessments found, agreed with the board and tracked to completion.
An independent, qualified outside review of the whole function, required at least once every five years.

subtopics.memory_aid: Internal results yearly, external on completion, always to both bodies.

topics.overview: Sometimes a requirement of the Standards cannot be met. This topic covers what the chief audit executive must document and tell, for the whole function and for one engagement, and the steps that take a nonconformance to senior management and the board.
can_do: Identify the four facts every nonconformance disclosure states
Tell a function-wide nonconformance from one in a single engagement, and name who hears each
Describe the steps from spotting a nonconformance to reporting and fixing it

subtopics.name: What a Nonconformance Disclosure Contains
subtopics.definition: A nonconformance disclosure is the chief audit executive's (CAE's) documented account of a requirement not met: the circumstance, the alternative actions taken, their impact and the reason.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Disclosure keeps the board's trust when full conformance is impossible. Hiding a gap, or claiming conformance anyway, misleads everyone who relies on internal audit's work.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 4.1 Conformance with the Global Internal Audit Standards): when a requirement cannot be met, the CAE documents and communicates the four elements below.
Must: if a law blocks part of the Standards, conform with the rest and disclose it; if another body's rules are also used, cite them.
Should: take alternative actions aimed at the requirement's intent, so the function may still achieve the principle.
Must (Domain III): if the board or senior management will not provide an essential condition, the CAE explains, with examples, what its absence does to the function.
Must: if they agree the condition is not needed, the CAE writes down why and what replaces it.
Should: if they still disagree and the CAE concludes the function cannot conform, the CAE writes down their reasons and shares them with both bodies.

types.meaning: What happened and which requirement was not met
What was done instead to meet the requirement's intent
How the gap and the alternative affect the work and its reliability
Why the requirement could not be met

subtopics.example: A spending freeze law stops a Portuguese city council buying outside reviews for 18 months, delaying its external assessment. CAE Ines documents the requirement missed, the alternative (a full self-assessment), the impact and the legal reason, and tells the board and senior management.

review: Inspect each nonconformance record for all four required elements
Compare disclosed nonconformances with gaps found by quality assessments
Trace each disclosure to its communication to the board
evidence: Nonconformance register with circumstance, alternatives, impact and reason
Copy of the legal text that blocked the requirement
External assessor's report noting disclosed and undisclosed gaps
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive keep a nonconformance register and report each entry to the board and senior management promptly.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive documents and discloses; the board oversees the response

subtopics.isaca_rule: Cannot conform? Say so in full: circumstance, alternative actions, impact, rationale. A law that blocks one part never excuses the rest. Hiding the gap or claiming conformance anyway is never the answer.

exam_traps.trap: The law prevented conformance, so there is nothing to disclose.
exam_traps.why: Must: conform with every other part of the Standards and make appropriate disclosures about the part the law prevents.

exam_traps.trap: A nonconformance can wait for the external assessor to find and report it.
exam_traps.why: Must: the CAE documents and communicates it. The external assessment then uses that record; it never replaces the disclosure.

key_terms.definition: A requirement of the Standards that was not met; it is documented and disclosed as the Standards direct.
A phrase in The IIA's Topical Requirements Application Guidance (guidance, not a rule): conformance is expected; if not feasible, take alternative actions and disclose why.

subtopics.memory_aid: Circumstance, alternative, impact, reason: all four, every time.

subtopics.name: Steps for Telling Senior Management and the Board
subtopics.definition: Communicating a nonconformance follows its reach: a gap in one engagement goes in that final communication; a function-wide gap goes to the board and senior management.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The right audience is whoever relies on the affected work. A gap in one report misleads its readers; a function-wide gap undermines every conclusion the board receives.
how_it_works: Should (Standard 4.1): an internal auditor who cannot conform tells the chief audit executive (CAE) or a designated supervisor why and with what effect; they advise on reporting.
Must (Standard 15.1 Final Engagement Communication): a nonconforming engagement's final communication names the standards missed, the reasons and the impact on findings and conclusions.
Should: the conformance statement fits only when supervision and the quality program support it, so it is left out for that engagement.
Must (Standard 12.1 Internal Quality Assessment): a nonconformance affecting the function's overall scope or operation goes, with its impact, to the board and senior management.
Must: build action plans with a timeline for nonconformances found in self-assessments, and report them and progress to the board and senior management.

rows.label: Where disclosed
cells: In that engagement's final communication
To the board and senior management directly

rows.label: What is stated
cells: Standards missed, reasons, impact on findings and conclusions
The nonconformance and its impact, with the Standard 4.1 elements

rows.label: Follow-up
cells: Cause fixed through supervision, staffing or methodology
Action plan with a timeline; progress reported

subtopics.example: In a payroll audit at a Uruguayan dairy cooperative, auditor Rosa finds the work program was never approved before testing. CAE Diego has the final report name the standard missed, why, and how it limits the conclusions. When a self-assessment finds the same gap in four engagements, Diego discloses it to the board and senior management.

review: Sample final communications where supervision found gaps for disclosure wording
Compare reports carrying the conformance statement with quality review results
Trace function-wide gaps to board and senior management reports
evidence: Final communications containing nonconformance disclosures
Supervision records showing engagements that did not conform
Board minutes recording function-wide gaps and action plans
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set a protocol that routes engagement and function-wide gaps to the right audience.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management receive function-wide disclosures and oversee fixes

subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the disclosure to the gap's reach: one engagement, in its final communication; the whole function, to the board and senior management with its impact. The conformance statement belongs only on work shown to conform (a should).

exam_traps.trap: A function-wide nonconformance goes to senior management only.
exam_traps.why: Must: a nonconformance affecting the function's overall scope or operation goes, with its impact, to both the board and senior management.

exam_traps.trap: Keep the conformance sentence; the gap is minor.
exam_traps.why: Should: the statement fits only work that supervision and the quality program show conformed. Must: disclose the standard missed, the reason and the impact.

key_terms.definition: A supervisor designated to act for the chief audit executive, for example to receive impairment disclosures.
A final-communication sentence saying the engagement was conducted in conformance with the Standards; it should appear only when supervision and quality program results support it.

subtopics.memory_aid: One engagement: in its report. Whole function: to the board and senior management.

topics.overview: Performance measures tell the board and senior management whether the function delivers what its mandate, charter and strategy promise. This topic covers why the chief audit executive sets them, how indicators and targets are chosen, and how to read the function's results.
can_do: Identify what the function's performance objectives and indicators are meant to show
Identify what to weigh when choosing an indicator, and why each needs a target
Explain why a balanced set mixes numbers with judgments, and spot measures that harm objectivity
Analyze a set of the function's measures and say what they reveal

subtopics.name: Why the Function Measures Its Performance
subtopics.definition: Performance objectives are the results the internal audit function commits to achieve; indicators, often called key performance indicators (KPIs), track progress toward them.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without objectives and measures, neither the chief audit executive nor the board can tell whether the function fulfills its mandate or improves. Measures turn quality from opinion into evidence.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 12.2 Performance Measurement): the chief audit executive (CAE) develops objectives to evaluate the function, considering the board's and senior management's input and expectations.
Must: set a method to assess progress and promote continuous improvement, seek feedback from the board and senior management, and act on issues with an action plan.

Essential condition (for the board or senior management, not a requirement on internal audit): the board approves the performance objectives at least annually and assesses the function with senior management.
Should: draw objectives from the Principles, the internal audit charter and the function's strategy, so measures show progress on what was promised.
subtopics.example: The audit committee of a Japanese electronics maker asks CAE Haruto how it will know internal audit is improving. Haruto drafts four objectives from the charter and strategy, gathers views from the chief executive and finance director, proposes a measure and target for each, and brings them to the committee for approval.

review: Trace each performance objective to the charter, strategy or Principles
Inspect board minutes for annual approval of the objectives
Compare missed targets with the action plans that followed
evidence: Board-approved performance objectives showing the approval date
Performance reports showing measures against targets
Feedback gathered from board members and executives
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive refresh the objectives with stakeholder input and put them to the board every year.
audit_focus.decides: Yearly sign-off of the objectives belongs to the board

subtopics.isaca_rule: The CAE develops the objectives and the measures; the board approves the objectives at least yearly, with senior management's input. Measures exist to show progress and drive improvement, so a shortfall needs an action plan.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE sets performance objectives alone, because board involvement would harm independence.
exam_traps.why: Must: the CAE considers the board's and senior management's input, and the board approves the objectives at least annually (an essential condition).

exam_traps.trap: Measuring is enough; the results are simply filed.
exam_traps.why: Must: the CAE develops an action plan for the issues and improvement opportunities the measures reveal.

key_terms.definition: A result the internal audit function commits to achieve, approved by the board at least annually.
Common usage: a short set of indicators, with targets and results, that the CAE reports to the board.

subtopics.name: Choosing Indicators and Setting Targets
subtopics.definition: Choosing indicators means picking a balanced set of measures for each objective, each with a target, mixing counts with judgments about quality and value.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A badly chosen indicator rewards the wrong behavior. Counting findings or hours alone can make the function look busy while it misses key risks or damages its objectivity.
how_it_works: Should (Standard 12.2 Performance Measurement): set quantitative and qualitative targets for each objective; a measure with no target cannot show success or shortfall.
Should: spread objectives across several areas, such as stakeholder expectations, wider conclusions, staffing, efficiency in money and operations, and auditor development.
May: report a focused set to the board and keep a fuller set for managing the function.
Should: check the accuracy of reported measures periodically and raise expectations over time.
Should (Standard 2.2): avoid judging or paying auditors mainly on findings counts, the audited area's revenue or savings, or its managers' ratings.
KaiSip's reading: numbers are easy to trend and compare; judgments capture value and insight that numbers miss, so a balanced set needs both.

rows.label: Example
cells: Percent of the approved plan done on time
Board satisfaction with the clarity of conclusions

rows.label: Strength
cells: Objective and comparable over time
Shows value, relevance and relationships

rows.label: Weakness
cells: Can reward volume over value
Harder to verify; needs clear rating criteria

subtopics.example: A Polish bank's internal audit scorecard counted only findings raised and hours charged. New CAE Zofia drops the findings count, which could push auditors to inflate issues, and adds key risks covered and board satisfaction, with targets: 90 percent of key risks reviewed over three years and an average rating of four out of five.

review: Inspect each indicator for a defined target and data source
Compare the spread of indicators across the outcome areas of Standard 12.2
Identify measures that tie auditor pay to findings counts or managers' ratings
evidence: Recomputed indicator values traced to source records
Indicator definitions with targets, owners and data sources
Evaluation and pay criteria for internal auditors
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive give every indicator a target and drop measures that could impair objectivity.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the objectives the indicators track

subtopics.isaca_rule: Every indicator needs a target, and the set needs balance: numbers for trend, judgments for value. Avoid measures that reward findings counts or the audited managers' approval (a should under Standard 2.2).

exam_traps.trap: The number of findings per auditor is the best single measure of audit performance.
exam_traps.why: Judging auditors by findings counts can impair objectivity (Standard 2.2 considerations). Value lies in coverage of key risks and the improvement achieved.

exam_traps.trap: Qualitative measures are too subjective to report to the board.
exam_traps.why: Should: set both quantitative and qualitative targets. Satisfaction and insight show value that numbers alone miss.

key_terms.definition: The level of an indicator that counts as success, set in advance so results can be judged.
A measure the CAE uses to track the function's progress toward one performance objective.

subtopics.name: Reading the Function's Performance Measures
subtopics.definition: Analyzing performance measures means reading the function's effectiveness, efficiency, productivity, quality, financial and operational results together to judge how it performs and what to improve.
subtopics.why_it_matters: One number can mislead: a plan finished on time may hide that key risks went untested. Reading measures together shows whether the function is busy, good or both.
how_it_works: KaiSip's reading: the table sorts example measures from Standards 8.3, 12.1 and 12.2 into the syllabus's categories; the Standards label only productivity and cost efficiency.
Sound practice: read measures in pairs; a cost or speed gain counts only if coverage and quality held up.
Sound practice: compare results with targets and trends over several periods; one miss may be noise, a steady slide is a signal.
Sound practice: trace a weak result to its cause, such as staffing, method or scope, before choosing the fix.
KaiSip's reading (Standard 12.2): action plan completion reflects management's follow-through as well as internal audit's work.

rows.label: Financial
cells: Budget-to-actual variance; cost efficiency
Coverage, so savings do not come from skipped risks

rows.label: Productivity and operational
cells: Planned against actual hours; audit against administrative time
Quality review results

rows.label: Quality
cells: External assessment conformance; certified staff
Stakeholder feedback

rows.label: Effectiveness
cells: Percent of key risks reviewed; actions achieving the desired outcome
Percent of the plan completed

rows.label: Efficiency
cells: Timeliness of engagements and reports
Accuracy and clarity of reports

subtopics.example: A Nigerian telecom's scorecard shows the whole plan finished on time and costs 8 percent under budget. CAE Chidinma looks further: key-risk coverage fell from 70 to 45 percent because a budget cut removed two cyber engagements. Chidinma reports both measures to the board and proposes how to restore coverage.

review: Recompute two or three reported indicators from source data
Compare each indicator's trend with its target over several periods
Analyze pairs of measures for gains bought with lost coverage
evidence: Time records and budget reports behind productivity and cost figures
Coverage map of key risks reviewed against the risk assessment
Stakeholder survey results with response rates
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive report paired measures to the board, with causes and action plans for weak results.
audit_focus.decides: The board judges the function's effectiveness and efficiency from these results

subtopics.isaca_rule: Read measures together, against targets and over time: efficiency gains count only if coverage and quality held. A weak result leads to cause analysis and an action plan.

exam_traps.trap: Finishing 100 percent of the plan on time proves the function is effective.
exam_traps.why: Plan completion shows output, and the Standards use it as one sign of efficiency and effectiveness. On its own it proves little: effectiveness also asks whether key risks were covered and conclusions improved governance, risk management and control.

exam_traps.trap: A low rate of completed action plans shows internal audit is performing poorly.
exam_traps.why: Management owns completing actions, so the rate reflects management's follow-through as well as internal audit's work.

key_terms.definition: A measure of output for the effort used, such as audit hours against total hours.
A measure of whether the function achieves its purpose, such as the share of key risks reviewed.

subtopics.memory_aid: Busy is not good: pair every speed measure with a coverage measure.

key_terminologies.Chief audit executive (CAE): The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
key_terminologies.Board: The highest governing body, such as the directors or audit committee; where several govern, the body (or bodies) empowered to give internal audit its mandate.
key_terminologies.Senior management: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.
key_terminologies.Conformance: Meeting the requirements of the Global Internal Audit Standards.
key_terminologies.Ongoing monitoring: Day-to-day supervision, review and measurement, built into how the function is run, that checks conformance and progress.
key_terminologies.Periodic self-assessment: A structured review, made at intervals by internal staff or others in the organization, of conformance with every standard.
key_terminologies.External quality assessment: An independent, qualified outside review of the whole function, required at least once every five years.
key_terminologies.Topical Requirement: A mandatory baseline for assurance engagements on a named subject, such as cybersecurity; recommended for advisory work.
key_terminologies.Quality assurance and improvement progra: The CAE's program of internal and external assessments covering conformance, performance objectives and continuous improvement.
key_terminologies.Quality: In the Standards' sense, meeting the Standards together with reaching the function's own performance goals.
key_terminologies.Fundamentals: The opening part of the Global Internal Audit Standards, explaining the framework and how to apply the Standards, small functions included.
key_terminologies.Internal assessment: The function's own check of its quality: ongoing monitoring plus periodic self-assessment, reported at least yearly.
key_terminologies.Stakeholder survey: A questionnaire asking those internal audit serves to rate its work; one input to ongoing monitoring.
key_terminologies.Consideration for Implementation: A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
key_terminologies.Self-assessment with independent validat: A full internal assessment that a qualified, independent outside assessor then validates; it can meet the external requirement.
key_terminologies.Reciprocal peer assessment: Two organizations' internal audit functions assessing each other; not independent for an external assessment.
key_terminologies.Essential conditions: Board and senior management activities, not requirements on them, that Domain III lists as necessary for an effective internal audit function.
key_terminologies.Domain III: The Standards' third domain, on governing the internal audit function: Principles 6 to 8 and Standards 6.1 to 8.4.
key_terminologies.Improvement plan: The CAE's dated actions to fix gaps that quality assessments found, agreed with the board and tracked to completion.
key_terminologies.Nonconformance: A requirement of the Standards that was not met; it is documented and disclosed as the Standards direct.
key_terminologies.Conform or explain: A phrase in The IIA's Topical Requirements Application Guidance (guidance, not a rule): conformance is expected; if not feasible, take alternative actions and disclose why.
key_terminologies.Designated supervisor: A supervisor designated to act for the chief audit executive, for example to receive impairment disclosures.
key_terminologies.Conformance statement: A final-communication sentence saying the engagement was conducted in conformance with the Standards; it should appear only when supervision and quality program results support it.
key_terminologies.Performance objective: A result the internal audit function commits to achieve, approved by the board at least annually.
key_terminologies.Scorecard: Common usage: a short set of indicators, with targets and results, that the CAE reports to the board.
key_terminologies.Target: The level of an indicator that counts as success, set in advance so results can be judged.
key_terminologies.Internal audit KPI: A measure the CAE uses to track the function's progress toward one performance objective.
key_terminologies.Productivity measure: A measure of output for the effort used, such as audit hours against total hours.
key_terminologies.Effectiveness measure: A measure of whether the function achieves its purpose, such as the share of key risks reviewed.
